title: Measuring Intra-horizon Value-at-Risk in Commodity Markets
affiliations: Southwest University of Finance and Economics, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Measuring Intra-horizon Value-at-Risk in Commodity Markets
detail.abstract: Traditional value-at-risk (VaR) and expected shortfall (ES) measures focusing on the endpoint loss may underestimate the risk induced by interim price movements. In this paper, we evaluate intra-horizon risk measures for energy and agricultural commodity markets, namely MaxVaR and MaxES, that reflect the maximum loss occurring at any time during a holding period with a given probability. We propose models with asymmetric jumps and/or seasonal volatility and generate out-of-sample MaxVaR and MaxES estimates over 10-, 22-, and 66-day horizons. Using data for heating oil, natural gas, corn, and soybeans from 2000 to 2021, we find that considering both jumps and seasonality leads to the most accurate MaxVaR and MaxES projections. Moreover, by comparing the intra-horizon risk measures with traditional ones, we document that the exposure resulted from ignoring the interim price movements increases with the horizon and requires a non-trivial amount of additional capital buffer to be prepared, especially for short positions. Finally, aiming at a more conservative confidence level in constructing traditional risk measures helps alleviate, although not eliminate, the capital adjustment needed to simultaneously manage the intra-horizon risk.

title: Radionuclide Transfer from Soil to Crops and Health Risk Assessment in Fertilized Farmlands of Benue State, Nigeria
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Ekiti State University

detail.title: Radionuclide Transfer from Soil to Crops and Health Risk Assessment in Fertilized Farmlands of Benue State, Nigeria
detail.abstract: This study investigates the transfer of radionuclides (238U, 232Th, 226Ra, and 40K) from soil to crops (cassava, maize, and okra) in Benue State, Nigeria, employing Transfer Factors (TFs) to quantify radionuclide uptake. A total of 90 crop-soil pairs were analyzed using a hyper-pure germanium detector. Results revealed that 40K exhibited the highest uptake across all crops. However, cassava showed concerning levels of uranium (238U) and radium (226Ra), with TFs of 0.09 and 0.42, respectively, surpassing safety thresholds set by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Radiological health risks were evaluated using ingestion dose models and Monte Carlo simulations (MCS) to estimate the Excess Lifetime Cancer Risk (ELCR). Indoor ELCR values ranged from 0.38 × 10−6 to 0.44 × 10−6, with maize showing the highest risk at 0.44 × 10−6, likely influenced by storage practices. Cassava posed a significant long-term ingestion risk due to elevated uranium and radium levels. Outdoor exposure resulted in an ELCR value of 0.11 × 10−6, while the total Ingestion Dose (IE) for all crops was calculated as 0.556 mSv y−1, which is below the acceptable radiation dose limit of 1 mSv per year for non-occupational exposure, it still represents a significant level of radiation intake that could pose potential health risks, particularly with long-term exposure, especially for crops like cassava with elevated levels of uranium and radium. These findings highlight the substantial radiological risks posed by crops radionuclide accumulation, and emphasize the urgent need for regular radionuclide monitoring in agricultural practices to mitigate long-term health risks and ensure food safety.

title: Environmental Regulation, Firm Emission Reaction, and Industrial Agglomeration: Evidence from China
affiliations: China Agricultural University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Environmental Regulation, Firm Emission Reaction, and Industrial Agglomeration: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: Environmental regulation policies may have differential effects on firms’ reaction of varying sizes, potentially leading to changes in industry structure—an effect often overlooked by policymakers and researchers. We construct a model to analyze firms’ reaction and industry structure under the general equilibrium, and then use the binding target of ammonia nitrogen emission reduction in the 12th Five-Year Plan as a quasi-experiment to test the theoretical conclusions, referring to the effect of environmental regulation shocks on firms’ pollution emissions and industry structure, as well as the mechanism channels. The results show that the effects of environmental regulation exhibit statistically significant heterogeneity among firms. The large firms, often with stronger governance, exhibit an improvement in their output, while the small firms decline. This ultimately causes industrial agglomeration within regulated industries. Tests of alternative competitive hypotheses show that the performance improvement of large firms is unrelated to the increase in industry agglomeration.

title: From Beliefs to Prices: Analyzing How Inflation Expectations Affect the Inflation Distribution
affiliations: Universidad San Sebastian, Pennsylvania State University Harrisburg, The University of Texas at Dallas and University of Texas at Dallas

detail.title: From Beliefs to Prices: Analyzing How Inflation Expectations Affect the Inflation Distribution
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how the distribution of inflation expectations influences realized inflation across its entire distribution. We find that shocks to median inflation expectations increase the median inflation rate for up to three years, and subsequently generate persistent upside risks in inflation that endure for more than six years. By analyzing higher-order moments; specifically, the standard deviation and skewness of inflation expectations, we show that greater disagreement among agents has distinct impacts on the distribution of the inflation rate. While an increase in the standard deviation amplifies right-tail inflation risks and generates quantile-dependent effects at the 90th percentile of the inflation distribution, a negative skewness shock temporarily shifts the distribution without any quantile-dependent effects. Our results highlight the critical importance of the distributional properties of inflation expectations for understanding and managing inflation risks. The results also underscore the need for well-anchored expectations to promote macroeconomic price stability.

title: Machine Learning for Detecting Collusion and Capacity Withholding in Wholesale Electricity Markets
affiliations: University of Fribourg and University of Fribourg

detail.title: Machine Learning for Detecting Collusion and Capacity Withholding in Wholesale Electricity Markets
detail.abstract: Collusion and capacity withholding in electricity wholesale markets are important mechanisms of market manipulation. This study applies a refined machine learning-based cartel detection algorithm to two cartel cases in the Italian electricity market and evaluates its out-of-sample performance. Specifically, we consider an ensemble machine learning method that uses statistical screens constructed from the offer price distribution as predictors for the incidence of collusion among electricity providers in specific regions. We propose novel screens related to the capacity-withholding behavior of electricity providers and find that including such screens derived from the day-ahead spot market as predictors can improve cartel detection. We find that, under complete cartels - where collusion in a tender presumably involves all suppliers - the method correctly classifies up to roughly 95% of tenders in our data as collusive or competitive, improving classification accuracy compared to using only previously available screens. However, when trained on larger datasets including non-cartel members and applying algorithms tailored to detect incomplete cartels, the previously existing screens are sufficient to achieve 98% accuracy, and the addition of our newly proposed capacity-withholding screens does not further improve performance. Overall, this study highlights the promising potential of supervised machine learning techniques for detecting and dismantling cartels in electricity markets.

title: Global and regional structural changes in energy systems and the broader economy under a net-zero emissions pathway
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Global and regional structural changes in energy systems and the broader economy under a net-zero emissions pathway
detail.abstract: Understanding structural changes in energy systems at global and regional levels is critical for informing policy, decision-making, and investment; this is particularly so in the context of achieving net-zero emissions as it entails significant systemic transformations. This study develops a methodological framework with a detailed guideline for linking global and national economic and energy models to examine the structural changes in energy systems and their impact on the Australian and global economy under the International Energy Agency’s Net Zero Emissions scenario. While the framework is applied to Australia in this work, it is adaptable to other regions and topics. Results indicate that both Australia and the global economy transition in a similar direction, with renewable energy accounting for over 90% of electricity generation by 2050. Industries significantly increase their demand for renewable electricity as a substitute for fossil fuels, the demand for which undergoes a substantial decline. Overall energy output contracts globally and in Australia, driven by higher production costs and significant improvements in energy efficiency; energy use per unit of output falls. Hydrogen emerges globally as a key energy carrier, particularly in electricity generation, chemical production, and transportation; in contrast Australia lags in this area despite its considerable potential to produce green hydrogen. Achieving net-zero targets incurs notable economic costs, with global (Australian) real GDP projected to fall by approximately 5% (4%) by 2050. These macroeconomic outcomes are sensitive to the pace at which the net-zero transition is implemented.

title: Climate Pay Incentives as a Driver of Climate Resilience International Evidence
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Climate Pay Incentives as a Driver of Climate Resilience International Evidence
detail.abstract: The worldwide efforts to improve firm sustainability have never been as intense as in recent years. Managerial compensation policies can play a pivotal role in achieving firm sustainability goals and reduce CO2 emissions. This article seeks to explore how businesses are weaving climate considerations into their managerial compensation strategies. Using an international sample from 58 countries in the post-COVID period, our results mainly reveal a significant and positive relationship between climate-linked compensation and climate resilience metrics. These results highlight the role of ESG-linked compensation as an effective incentive mechanism for promoting environmental corporate practices. Moreover, this relationship is moderated by the respect for international frameworks such as the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. Our findings are robust to several robustness checks.

reference: Libra Sentinel AI Literacy Series Working Paper
title: AI Guardrails - Spotting & Fixing Common LLM Failure Modes
affiliations: Libra Sentinel - Data Privacy & AI Governance

detail.title: AI Guardrails - Spotting & Fixing Common LLM Failure Modes

publicationDetails.detailsText: Libra Sentinel AI Literacy Series Working Paper

detail.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT are increasingly deployed in professional and compliance-sensitive environments. Yet these systems have recurring “failure modes” — predictable patterns of error that, if undetected, pose risks for accuracy, accountability, and regulatory compliance.

This paper presents a practical framework for identifying and mitigating three common LLM failure modes: hallucination/overconfidence, lost-in-the-middle degradation, and input truncation. For each, it provides contextual analysis, oversight relevance, and applied mitigation strategies in the form of guardrail prompts.

The guide aligns with Article 4 of the EU AI Act (AI literacy) by equipping staff and stakeholders with the skills, knowledge, and understanding to use AI systems responsibly. It further supports Article 14 (human oversight) by showing how AI-literate human involvement transforms oversight from a procedural checkbox into effective risk control.

The contribution is practice-oriented: enabling organizations and professionals to strengthen competence, compliance, and confidence when deploying AI systems.
